Daniel’s metaphor is vivid, but it smuggles in a strong assumption: that “who has eaten what” is primarily an information problem rather than a norm-governed social performance. At a Chinese roundtable, the person who notices you haven’t tried a dish is often acting in a host-like role—managing generosity, face, and inclusion—so the “matrix” is less a private database than a public duty enacted through timely prompts. That difference matters because it reframes the “ability” from cognitive superpower to social technology: attention deployed to signal care, coordinate turn-taking, and smooth status relations. Modeling it as a boolean grid also flattens what is usually continuous and strategic (portion size, reluctance, dietary constraints, deference, or the polite fiction that you “should” be urged even if you already sampled it). If Daniel intended this as a pure cognition puzzle, the post’s framing doesn’t clarify why it ignores those incentives; if he intended a culture/etiquette observation, the matrix metaphor may mislead readers into thinking it’s mainly about memory.

The “zero-knowledge proof” analogy is clever but slightly off in a way that’s illuminating. In cryptography, a ZKP lets a prover convince a verifier of a statement without revealing anything beyond its truth; here, telling you “you haven’t tried X” reveals the exact hidden fact (your non-consumption), and it typically also reveals something about the speaker’s attention model (they’ve been watching your plate, or at least tracking flows). A closer fit might be *selective disclosure*: the speaker reveals only what advances the interaction (a prompt) while keeping the underlying “ledger” implicit. If Daniel wants the crypto connection to do real work, he could tighten it by specifying what is supposedly kept secret (the full table-state? the observation process? the confidence level?), and by acknowledging that social proofs routinely trade privacy for care—an uncomfortable but central tension that the matrix metaphor, used straight, tends to sanitize. For readers curious about the genuine concept, the canonical definition is in [Goldwasser–Micali–Rackoff’s work on zero-knowledge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zero-knowledge_proof); for the social side Daniel is gesturing toward without naming, the relevant lineage runs through [Erving Goffman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erving_Goffman) and how interaction is “managed” rather than merely “known.”
